pairs.question: Will I notice any changes in my breathing after I quit?
pairs.answer: Yes! Coughing and shortness of breath decrease after you quit smoking. You'll likely feel a lot more comfortable breathing.
pairs.evidence: Coughing and shortness of breath decrease.

pairs.question: What about my heart health if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Your risk of heart attack drops dramatically after you quit smoking. That's a great reason to stop!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of heart attack drops dramatically.

pairs.question: How does quitting smoking affect my cancer risk?
pairs.answer: Your risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, and voice box (larynx) is cut in half after quitting. It's a significant reduction!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of cancers of the mouth, throat and voice box (larynx) is cut in half.

pairs.question: What happens to my risk of stroke if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Your risk of stroke decreases after you quit smoking. It's one of the many benefits of quitting!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of stroke decreases.

pairs.question: How does quitting affect my lung cancer risk?
pairs.answer: After quitting, your risk of lung cancer is about half that of a person who is still smoking. That's a huge improvement!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of lung cancer is about half that of a person who is still smoking.

pairs.question: What about my heart disease risk after I quit?
pairs.answer: Your risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of a nonsmoker after quitting. That's fantastic news for your health!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of a nonsmoker.

pairs.question: What happens to my risk of cancer if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Your risk of cancer of the bladder, esophagus, and kidney decreases. It's great to know that quitting can significantly lower your cancer risks!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of cancer of the bladder, esophagus, and kidney decreases.

pairs.question: How does quitting smoking affect my heart health?
pairs.answer: Your risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of a nonsmoker. That's a big improvement for your heart health!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of a nonsmoker.

pairs.question: Will my cancer risks drop if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Yes, your risk of several cancers, including those of the mouth, throat, voice box (larynx), and pancreas, drops to close to that of someone who does not smoke. Quitting really helps reduce those risks!
pairs.evidence: Your risk of several cancers, including those of the mouth, throat, voice box (larynx), and pancreas, drops to close to that of someone who does not smoke.

pairs.question: What about cervical cancer? Does quitting help?
pairs.answer: Your added risk of cervical cancer drops by about half if you quit smoking. That's a significant benefit!
pairs.evidence: Your added risk of cervical cancer drops by about half.

pairs.question: How does quitting smoking affect my overall cancer risk over time?
pairs.answer: Quitting smoking lowers your risk of other cancers over time, including cancers of the stomach, liver, cervix, colon, and rectum as well as acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It's a great step for your long-term health!
pairs.evidence: Quitting smoking lowers your risk of other cancers over time, including cancers of the stomach, liver, cervix, colon, and rectum as well as acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

pairs.question: What other health problems can quitting smoking help with?
pairs.answer: Quitting also lowers your risk of heart and lung problems such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung infections, and circulation around your heart and other body parts. That's a lot of health benefits!
pairs.evidence: Quitting also lowers your risk of heart and lung problems such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung infections, and circulation around your heart and other body parts.

pairs.question: How much longer can I live if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: People who quit smoking can also add as much as 10 years to their life, compared to people who continue to smoke. That's a huge incentive to quit!
pairs.evidence: People who quit smoking can also add as much as 10 years to their life, compared to people who continue to smoke.

pairs.question: Is it better to quit smoking when I'm younger?
pairs.answer: Yes, quitting before the age of 40 reduces the risk of dying from smoking-related disease by about 90%. But remember, quitting at any age can still give you back years of life!
pairs.evidence: Quitting while you're younger can reduce your health risks more (for example, quitting before the age of 40 reduces the risk of dying from smoking-related disease by about 90%).

pairs.question: What happens to my sense of smell if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Right away, your sense of smell returns to normal. It's one of the first benefits you'll notice after quitting. That's a great reason to stick with it!
pairs.evidence: Your sense of smell returns to normal.

pairs.question: Will I notice a difference in how I smell after quitting?
pairs.answer: Yes! Your breath, hair, and clothes smell better right after you quit. It's a nice change that many people appreciate.
pairs.evidence: Your breath, hair, and clothes smell better.

pairs.question: What about my teeth and nails? Will they change if I quit?
pairs.answer: Absolutely! Your teeth and fingernails stop yellowing after you quit smoking. It's a positive change for your appearance.
pairs.evidence: Your teeth and fingernails stop yellowing.

pairs.question: Will I feel less out of breath after quitting?
pairs.answer: Yes, ordinary activities like climbing stairs or light housework will leave you less out of breath. Quitting really helps with your stamina!
pairs.evidence: Ordinary activities (like climbing stairs or light housework) leave you less out of breath.

pairs.question: Can I be in smoke-free buildings without needing to go outside?
pairs.answer: Definitely! After you quit, you can be in smoke-free buildings without having to go outside to smoke. It's a freeing experience.
pairs.evidence: You can be in smoke-free buildings without having to go outside to smoke.

pairs.question: What is the best way to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: For most people, the best way to quit is some combination of medicine, a method to change personal habits, and emotional support. Finding what works for you is key!
pairs.evidence: For most people, the best way to quit is some combination of medicine, a method to change personal habits, and emotional support.

pairs.question: Is deciding to quit a big deal?
pairs.answer: Yes, deciding to quit tobacco is a major milestone. It's an important step towards a healthier life.
pairs.evidence: Deciding to quit tobacco is a major milestone.

pairs.question: What part of quitting is the most important?
pairs.answer: The final part of the process, staying tobacco-free after you quit, is the longest and most important. It's crucial to maintain your commitment.
pairs.evidence: But quit is the final, longest, and most important part of the process.
